::: {.content-hidden when-format="revealjs"}
### Getting a bipolar signal onto a unipolar ADC {#sec-s3-conditioning}
:::

::: {.content-visible when-format="revealjs"}
### Getting a bipolar signal onto a unipolar ADC (1)
:::

A signal generator's output is bipolar — it swings around 0 V — and an
Arduino analog input is not: it accepts $0$ to $V_\mathrm{io}$ and clips, or
worse, outside that range. Between the generator and the pin sits a
**conditioning stage** that does one linear thing,

$$
V_\mathrm{adc} = G\,V_\mathrm{in} + V_\mathrm{off}
$$ {#eq-s3-conditioning}

and the whole design problem is choosing $G$ and $V_\mathrm{off}$.

::: {.content-visible when-format="revealjs"}
### Getting a bipolar signal onto a unipolar ADC (2)
:::

Suppose the
generator is set to a peak (bipolar) amplitude $V_g$, so
$V_\mathrm{in} \in [-V_g, +V_g]$, and you want that interval to land on
$[V_\mathrm{lo}, V_\mathrm{hi}]$ at the ADC pin, with
$0 < V_\mathrm{lo} < V_\mathrm{hi} < V_\mathrm{io}$. Solving
@eq-s3-conditioning at the two endpoints gives

$$
G = \frac{V_\mathrm{hi} - V_\mathrm{lo}}{2\,V_g},
\qquad
V_\mathrm{off} = \frac{V_\mathrm{hi} + V_\mathrm{lo}}{2}
$$ {#eq-s3-gain-offset}

and recovering the input from a reading is the inverse map,

$$
\hat{V}_\mathrm{in} = \frac{V_\mathrm{adc} - V_\mathrm{off}}{G}
$$ {#eq-s3-recover}

::: {.content-visible when-format="revealjs"}
### Getting a bipolar signal onto a unipolar ADC (3)
:::

::: {.callout-important}
## Never design for exactly full scale

$V_\mathrm{lo}$ and $V_\mathrm{hi}$ should sit strictly inside $[0, V_\mathrm{io}]$,
not on the rails. Three things eat into the margin you leave: the
generator's own amplitude tolerance, the conditioning stage's own gain and
offset error (@eq-s3-gain-offset again, now as a source of error rather than
a design target), and any overshoot on a fast edge. A stage designed for
$V_\mathrm{hi}$ exactly at $V_\mathrm{io}$ clips the first time any of those
three pushes the signal a millivolt too far, and a clipped sample is not
noisy data — it is wrong data that looks like good data.
:::

::: {.content-visible when-format="revealjs"}
### Getting a bipolar signal onto a unipolar ADC (4)
:::

The reference data shipped with this experiment uses
$V_\mathrm{lo} = 0.3$ V and $V_\mathrm{hi} = 3.0$ V against
$V_\mathrm{io} = 3.3$ V — 0.3 V of headroom at each rail — for a generator set
to $V_g = 1.0$ V. @eq-s3-gain-offset then gives $G = 1.35$ and
$V_\mathrm{off} = 1.65$ V; see [the conditioning board](../../hardware/conditioning-board.qmd)
for how a resistor network realizes this pair of numbers, and
`tools/synth/params/s3.yaml` for where these values live in the generator.

::: {.content-hidden when-format="revealjs"}
$V_\mathrm{off} = V_\mathrm{io}/2$ here only because the headroom was chosen
symmetric; nothing about @eq-s3-gain-offset requires that, and an input stage
that itself has an offset error would want the two margins unequal so the
worst case is still inside $[0, V_\mathrm{io}]$.
:::

::: {.content-visible when-format="revealjs"}
### Getting a bipolar signal onto a unipolar ADC (5)
:::

#### Uncertainty of the conditioned reading {#sec-s3-conditioning-uncertainty}

$G$ and $V_\mathrm{off}$ are not exact: they are set by real resistors and a
real amplifier, each with its own tolerance, and that uncertainty does not
stay upstream — it multiplies and adds to every reading downstream of it. The
sensitivity coefficients of @eq-s3-recover, needed for the budget, are

$$
\frac{\partial \hat{V}_\mathrm{in}}{\partial V_\mathrm{adc}} = \frac{1}{G},
\qquad
\frac{\partial \hat{V}_\mathrm{in}}{\partial V_\mathrm{off}} = -\frac{1}{G},
\qquad
\frac{\partial \hat{V}_\mathrm{in}}{\partial G} =
-\frac{V_\mathrm{adc} - V_\mathrm{off}}{G^{2}}
$$ {#eq-s3-sensitivity-cond}

::: {.content-hidden when-format="revealjs"}
The last term is the one worth staring at: it is zero only when
$V_\mathrm{adc} = V_\mathrm{off}$, at the centre of the range, and grows
linearly with distance from it. A gain error contributes nothing to the
uncertainty of a mid-scale reading and the most it ever will at the extremes
of the range — the same shape of effect as
[S1's sensitivity coefficients](../S1-daq-static/handbook.qmd#eq-s1-sensitivity),
and for the same reason: both are multiplicative errors evaluated about a
mean of zero.

If $G$ is realized as a resistive divider or a difference amplifier built
from two resistors of tolerance $\varepsilon$ each, the fractional
uncertainty of $G$ from the resistors alone is of order $\varepsilon\sqrt{2}$
(two independent tolerances in quadrature) before adding the amplifier's own
gain error and the reference's own tolerance; the offset uncertainty
similarly gets a contribution from every resistor and reference voltage that
sets $V_\mathrm{off}$. No specific resistor values are assumed here — see
[the conditioning board](../../hardware/conditioning-board.qmd) for the
circuit once it exists — so both $u(G)$ and $u(V_\mathrm{off})$ are carried as
placeholders in `tools/synth/params/s3.yaml`, marked `TODO (Paolo)`, until a
real network is characterized.
:::

::: {.content-hidden when-format="revealjs"}
### Aliasing: what a slow sample rate does to a fast signal {#sec-s3-aliasing}
:::

::: {.content-visible when-format="revealjs"}
### Aliasing: what a slow sample rate does to a fast signal (1) {#sec-s3-aliasing-deck}
:::

Sample a sinusoid of frequency $f$ at a rate $f_s < 2f$ and the sequence of
numbers you get back is indistinguishable from a sinusoid at a lower
frequency $f_a$. Which lower frequency is deterministic:

$$
f_a = \left| f - k f_s \right|, \qquad k = \operatorname{round}\!\left(\frac{f}{f_s}\right)
$$ {#eq-s3-alias}

$k$ counts how many multiples of $f_s$ have to be added to or subtracted from
$f$ to fold it into $[0, f_s/2]$. As $f$ sweeps upward past each multiple of
$f_s/2$, $f_a$ retraces $[0, f_s/2]$ — up, down, up, down — which is why
plotting $f_a$ against $f$ for a sweep of generator frequencies produces a
triangle wave, the **folding triangle**, with period $f_s$.

::: {.content-visible when-format="revealjs"}
### Aliasing: what a slow sample rate does to a fast signal (2)
:::

::: {.callout-warning}
## Aliasing is not a measurement error you can find in the data

A component that has folded to $f_a$ and a real signal at $f_a$ produce
*exactly the same samples*. There is no test on the recorded numbers alone
that tells them apart — no amount of averaging, filtering or clever
statistics recovers the information that was lost at the instant of
sampling, because @eq-s3-alias is many-to-one: every $f_a$ has infinitely many
$f = k f_s \pm f_a$ that produce it. This is the single most important fact
in this experiment, and it is the reason the next section exists: the only
place aliasing can be *prevented* is before the sampler, never after.
:::

::: {.content-hidden when-format="revealjs"}
### Anti-alias filtering: a design decision, not a fix {#sec-s3-filter}
:::

::: {.content-visible when-format="revealjs"}
### Anti-alias filtering: a design decision, not a fix (1)
:::

An anti-alias filter is an analog low-pass filter placed ahead of the ADC so
that whatever would fold into the band of interest is attenuated before it
has the chance. This experiment uses the maximally-flat, Butterworth-style
magnitude response

$$
|H(f)| = \frac{1}{\sqrt{1 + (f/f_c)^{2n}}}
$$ {#eq-s3-filter-mag}

for an $n$-pole filter with corner (−3 dB) frequency $f_c$ — stated
explicitly because it is a choice: the exact transfer function of $n$
cascaded passive RC stages is a different, messier expression once each stage
loads the one before it, and does not roll off as cleanly.

::: {.content-visible when-format="revealjs"}
### Anti-alias filtering: a design decision, not a fix (2)
:::

@eq-s3-filter-mag
is what you get from $n$ stages each buffered by an op-amp (unity-gain or
otherwise), so that each stage sees a true voltage source and the stages'
responses simply multiply; a first-order stage is @eq-s3-filter-mag with
$n=1$, and needs no buffering to behave this way on its own.

::: {.content-hidden when-format="revealjs"}
Two bare RC stages in series, with no buffer between them, do **not** give
$n = 2$ in @eq-s3-filter-mag: the second stage's input impedance loads the
first stage's output, pulling the combined response away from maximally flat
and closer to two staggered real poles. An op-amp voltage follower between
the stages restores the assumption that each RC sees an ideal source, which
is the only reason @eq-s3-filter-mag is exact rather than approximate for
$n > 1$ here.
:::

Because the filter acts on the continuous-time signal, the attenuation that
matters for a folded component is $|H(f)|$ evaluated at the **true**
frequency $f$, not at the apparent frequency $f_a$ it will fold to — the
filter has no way to know where a component will end up.

::: {.content-visible when-format="revealjs"}
### Anti-alias filtering: a design decision, not a fix (3)
:::

#### Designing $f_c$ and $n$ against a required attenuation {#sec-s3-filter-design}

Suppose signals up to $f_\mathrm{max}$ are of interest, sampled at $f_s$, and
you require at least $A$ dB of attenuation for anything at or above the
frequency $f_\mathrm{fold}$ that would fold into $[0, f_\mathrm{max}]$ — in
the worst case, $f_\mathrm{fold} = f_s - f_\mathrm{max}$. Inverting
@eq-s3-filter-mag in decibels,

$$
A = 10\log_{10}\!\left[1 + \left(\frac{f_\mathrm{fold}}{f_c}\right)^{2n}\right]
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
f_c = \frac{f_\mathrm{fold}}{\left(10^{A/10} - 1\right)^{1/(2n)}}
$$ {#eq-s3-design-fc}

::: {.content-visible when-format="revealjs"}
### Anti-alias filtering: a design decision, not a fix (4)
:::

and the price is paid in the passband, where the same expression evaluated at
$f_\mathrm{max}$ gives the droop,

$$
\mathrm{droop}(f_\mathrm{max}) =
-10\log_{10}\!\left[1 + \left(\frac{f_\mathrm{max}}{f_c}\right)^{2n}\right]\ \mathrm{dB}
$$ {#eq-s3-droop}

::: {.content-hidden when-format="revealjs"}
Work an example with the numbers this experiment's sampled runs use:
$f_s = 500$ Hz, a passband up to $f_\mathrm{max} = 150$ Hz, and a modest
target of $A = 20$ dB at the worst-case fold frequency
$f_\mathrm{fold} = 500 - 150 = 350$ Hz. @eq-s3-design-fc with $n = 2$ gives
$f_c \approx 111$ Hz — already inside the passband — and @eq-s3-droop then
gives a droop at 150 Hz of about $-6.4$ dB, more than a factor of two down at
the top of the band you claimed to preserve. Push $f_c$ back out to 150 Hz
(the edge of the passband, the usual place to put a Butterworth corner) and
the attenuation at 350 Hz falls to about $-14.9$ dB, short of the 20 dB
target. Two poles cannot deliver both a flat 150 Hz passband and 20 dB at
350 Hz — they are less than one octave apart, and each pole only buys 6 dB
per octave. The only way out is more poles ($n$ larger, at the cost of more
op-amps and more design margin against instability) or more separation
between $f_\mathrm{max}$ and $f_\mathrm{fold}$, which usually means sampling
faster.

This is the general shape of every anti-alias design: attenuation at the fold
frequency and flatness in the passband trade directly against $n$ and against
how far apart $f_\mathrm{max}$ and $f_\mathrm{fold}$ are allowed to be.
:::

::: {.content-visible when-format="revealjs"}
### Anti-alias filtering: a design decision, not a fix (5)
:::

The [filtered/unfiltered pair shipped with this experiment](index.qmd#sec-s3-index-data)
instead demonstrates the *effect* of a filter rather than solving this
trade-off: a 2-pole filter with $f_c = 100$ Hz applied to a 650 Hz tone that
would otherwise alias to 150 Hz at $f_s = 500$ Hz. @eq-s3-filter-mag at
$f = 650$ Hz gives $|H| \approx 0.0237$, about $-32.5$ dB — the aliased
component survives filtering (the filter cannot know it is about to alias)
but at roughly 1/42 of its unfiltered amplitude, well down toward, though
not fully into, the ADC's own noise floor characterized in
[S1](../S1-daq-static/index.qmd).

::: {.content-visible when-format="revealjs"}
### Anti-alias filtering: a design decision, not a fix (6)
:::

::: {.callout-note}
## How the filter is modelled in the generated data

The reference data does not simulate an RC network in continuous time; it
generates the sinusoid, multiplies its amplitude by the scalar
$|H(f)|$ of @eq-s3-filter-mag at the generator's own frequency, and only then
runs it through the conditioning stage and the ADC model. This is the honest
model of an analog filter acting on a *single* sinusoid — amplitude scaling
and a phase shift, nothing else — and it is exact for the filtered/unfiltered
pair because that pair uses exactly one tone. It would not be adequate for a
non-sinusoidal or multi-tone signal, which is why the oversampled run below
is filtered *digitally*, sample by sample, rather than by scaling.
:::

::: {.content-hidden when-format="revealjs"}
### Digital filtering after the fact {#sec-s3-digital}
:::

::: {.content-visible when-format="revealjs"}
### Digital filtering after the fact (1)
:::

A digital low-pass filter, applied to already-sampled data, removes energy
above its cutoff exactly as an analog filter would — provided nothing has
folded yet. Filter an **oversampled** recording (sampled comfortably above
twice the highest frequency present) and decimate it down, and the result is
clean: the interferer never had the chance to alias, so removing it digitally
before decimating is equivalent to having filtered it in analog before
sampling in the first place.

::: {.content-visible when-format="revealjs"}
### Digital filtering after the fact (2)
:::

Filter an **undersampled** recording the same way and nothing improves,
because [@sec-s3-aliasing]{.content-hidden when-format="revealjs"}[@sec-s3-aliasing-deck]{.content-visible when-format="revealjs"} already established the reason: the samples of a
folded component and the samples of a real signal at $f_a$ are the same
numbers. A digital filter with a passband that includes $f_a$ passes the
alias through exactly as it would pass a genuine signal, because at the level
of the sample sequence there is no difference for it to detect.

$$
\underbrace{f > f_s/2,\ \text{filtered digitally after sampling}}_{\text{too late: already folded to } f_a}
\qquad\text{vs.}\qquad
\underbrace{f > f_s/2,\ \text{filtered in analog before sampling}}_{\text{attenuated at the true frequency } f, \text{ never folds}}
$$

: Where a low-pass filter has to sit to do anything about a component above
$f_s/2$ {#tbl-s3-filter-timing}

::: {.content-visible when-format="revealjs"}
### Digital filtering after the fact (3) {.smaller}
:::

#### The filter used here: an explicit windowed-sinc FIR {#sec-s3-fir}

Both analysis templates need to apply *the same* digital filter and get *the
same* numbers. A library-designed IIR filter (a Butterworth via bilinear
transform, applied with zero-phase forward-backward filtering) turned out not
to satisfy that in practice: `scipy.signal.butter` + `filtfilt` in Python and
`gsignal::butter` + `filtfilt` in R design matching coefficients but differ in
their edge padding, and the disagreement — a few percent near the ends of a
short record — is large enough to break table-for-table agreement between the
two templates. Both languages instead compute an explicit **windowed-sinc FIR
filter**, from a closed-form formula rather than a library call, and apply it
by direct convolution:

$$
h[n] = \frac{w[n]\,\operatorname{sinc}\!\left(\dfrac{2 f_c}{f_s}(n - M)\right)}
            {\displaystyle\sum_{m=0}^{L-1} w[m]\,\operatorname{sinc}\!\left(\dfrac{2 f_c}{f_s}(m - M)\right)},
\qquad M = \frac{L-1}{2}
$$ {#eq-s3-fir}

::: {.content-visible when-format="revealjs"}
### Digital filtering after the fact (4)
:::

with $L$ taps, a Hamming window $w[n] = 0.54 - 0.46\cos(2\pi n/(L-1))$, and
$\operatorname{sinc}(x) = \sin(\pi x)/(\pi x)$ (and $1$ at $x = 0$); the
denominator normalizes the passband gain to unity. Filtering is the direct
sum

$$
y[n] = \sum_{k=0}^{L-1} h[k]\,x[n-k]
$$ {#eq-s3-fir-output}

computed only where the full window of $L$ input samples exists (a "valid"
convolution), so both languages carry out the same difference equation on the
same numbers with no filter-design library, and no edge-handling convention,
left to disagree.

::: {.content-hidden when-format="revealjs"}
### Relation to S1 and S2 {#sec-s3-relation}
:::

::: {.content-visible when-format="revealjs"}
### Relation to S1 and S2 (1)
:::

Neither aliasing nor filtering exists in a vacuum on this bench. Two numbers
from earlier experiments set the terms this experiment's conclusions are
judged against:

- The effective resolution measured in [S1](../S1-daq-static/index.qmd) — the
  [ENOB](../S1-daq-static/handbook.qmd#eq-s1-enob) and the noise floor behind it — is the floor a filter's
  attenuation is compared with. A component attenuated by 40 dB is not "gone"
  if it started 60 dB above the noise floor; it is still there at 20 dB above
  it. Attenuation is only ever attenuation *relative to* something, and S1 is
  what supplies that something for every experiment after it.

::: {.content-visible when-format="revealjs"}
### Relation to S1 and S2 (2)
:::

- The sampling-grid quality measured in [S2](../S2-daq-dynamic/index.qmd) sets
  how well an apparent frequency can be estimated at all: a grid with
  microsecond-level jitter measures a 150 Hz tone precisely, but the same
  jitter as a *fraction of the period* grows at higher apparent frequencies,
  and S2's dynamic ENOB is the more relevant comparison than S1's static one
  whenever the signal of interest is moving, which in this experiment it
  always is.
